item.title: MADlibs: Analyzing the Distribution of Generative Music
item.description: arXiv:2611.31462v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: What music can a text-to-music model actually make? The answer to this question has consequences for individual creators, communities, and musical culture more broadly. We introduce MADlibs, a framework to measure the expressive support of state-of-the-art music generators: the subset of musical behaviors they will actually produce across the space of prompts. We first develop strategies for generating musical prompts using natural language processing methods and existing caption corpora. Then, we use a set of MIR techniques to study the corresponding output spaces in terms of interpretable and qualitatively meaningful elements like key, beat, tempo, instrumentation, and dynamics. We find that text-to-music models are not interchangeable instruments for the same prompt space. Rather, each model has learned idiosyncratic properties that constrain the regime of music reachable via prompting it, for example, defaulting to certain tempi, failing to produce silences, or oversampling canonical band arrangements. Because users interact with these systems one prompt at a time, these biases are often invisible in practice yet cumulatively shape what AI-assisted music sounds like, risking the production of a new auditory monoculture hidden behind the promise of universal describability. We thus urge the MIR community to further study and responsibly steer population-level properties of music generation models.
item.dc:creator: Matthew Keating, Noah Schaffer, Michael Casey, Nikhil Singh

item.title: IncrementDET: Continual AI-Generated Music Detection via Enrollment
item.description: arXiv:2611.32023v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: AI-generated music has become common on music streaming platforms, and listeners often cannot distinguish it from music made by humans. AI-music detection is therefore needed, but detectors trained on a fixed set of generators often fail on unseen generators. As new generators emerge frequently, updating a universal detector, a single model for all generators, typically requires substantial training data and computation, while risking performance degradation on previously learned generators. We therefore introduce IncrementDET, a detector that learns each new generator by a process called enrollment. For each generator, IncrementDET trains one linear classifier, which we call a needle, to separate samples of that generator from a fixed set of human reference tracks. Enrolling a new generator adds one needle while the previously constructed needles remain unchanged. A Sidak correction keeps the overall false-positive rate at its target as needles are added. To compare detectors under these conditions, we define the task of continual AI-generated music detection and introduce a benchmark in which generators arrive one at a time. The benchmark measures the accuracy of a detector before and after each update and the cost of each update. For this benchmark, we also construct EvoMusicFake-17K, a dataset of instrumental music from six recent generators and four human music platforms. Compared with SpecTTTra, a state-of-the-art universal detector, IncrementDET learns a new generator more accurately from only a few samples, generalizes better to unseen generators and better preserves detection performance on previously learned generators, at a substantially lower update cost. The structure of IncrementDET can also be applied to the detection of generated images and video, where new generators are released just as frequently.
item.dc:creator: Runbao Du, Wei Li, Qile He

item.title: Reproducing the Speech Labels of Qwen3-Omni's Talker: Mimi in bf16, and a Last-Frame Pitfall
item.description: arXiv:2611.32286v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Qwen3-Omni speaks through a Talker predicting 16 codebooks of a 12.5 Hz audio codec, but the encoder that made its training labels was not released, so new voices cannot be trained on matching labels. We identify this encoder from the released model's behavior. White-box regression shows that the codebook embeddings of the Talker, its multi-token predictor and the Code2Wav decoder match the first 16 codebooks of kyutai's Mimi layer by layer. A decoder-based test looks convincing but fails calibration: decoders trained on known labels cannot tell them apart. Teacher-forced Talker likelihoods, calibrated with 13 code language models trained on known labels, do tell implementations apart: the Talker prefers labels from kyutai's moshi package with bf16 weights over every other variant we tried. Loudness normalization and band-limiting of 20% or more of the data are ruled out. Separately, transformers' MimiModel encodes the last frame differently from kyutai's encoder unless the input length is a multiple of 1920 samples. After LoRA fine-tuning on its labels, 44--55% of generated sentences end in a noise burst, and the same frame costs the Mimi-based CSM-1B 119 nats; padding the input removes both. We release the encoding recipe, a label checker and a Talker fine-tuning toolkit.
item.dc:creator: Yuxuan Chen

item.title: Do Layer Rankings Survive Silence Trimming? The Silence Shortcut in Frozen WavLM Representations for Audio Deepfake Detection
item.description: arXiv:2611.32457v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Layer-wise analyses of frozen self-supervised encoders are used to locate spoofing information in audio deepfake detection. On the ASVspoof 2019 logical access (LA) benchmark, bonafide recordings carry longer leading and trailing silence than spoofed ones, and detectors exploit this cue, the silence shortcut. This paper examines whether layer rankings for a frozen WavLM Base encoder survive the trimming of this silence. A small classifier is trained on each of the 12 layers with and without trimming and evaluated on ASVspoof 2019 LA and, zero-shot, on In-the-Wild, in all four train/test combinations, with speaker-level bootstrap intervals. Trimming at 40 dB raises the in-domain error at every layer and preserves the layer ranking only partly (Kendall's tau of 0.58 in domain, 0.73-0.76 on In-the-Wild). The best layer is unchanged at 40 dB, but on the evaluation set it moves from layer 5 to layer 6 at 15 dB and, with mean pooling, at 20 dB, thresholds at which trimming may also remove low-energy speech. At 40 dB, the equal error rate of a model trained with silence rises by 6.3-19.9 percentage points at every layer when only its test audio is trimmed. On In-the-Wild, the effect depends on the layer: at layers 3-5, trimming the test audio lowers the error only for models trained on trimmed audio, whereas at layers 6, 8, and 9 training on trimmed audio lowers it also on clean test audio. We quantify how zero padding alters WavLM features through group normalization, an effect that an attention mask does not fully undo.
item.dc:creator: Nur Elabid, Mahmud Esad Arar

item.title: VividAudio: Multi-Event Reference-Conditioned Video-to-Audio Generation
item.description: arXiv:2611.32458v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Existing video-to-audio (V2A) methods have achieved promising results in synthesizing high-quality audios. However, as V2A advances toward more flexible user-directed creation, existing methods remain notably limited in controlling the distinct acoustic identities of multiple events within a video. We therefore formulate multi-event reference-conditioned V2A (Mr-V2A), where each event is assigned a specific audio reference and target time span. Mr-V2A presents three key challenges. First, event-level reference-target training pairs are scarce. We introduce Intra-Video Event Variation (IntraEvtVar), which constructs non-oracle pairs through four variation modes of events mined within each video. Second, we organize the references into a Time-Aligned COmposite Reference (TACO-Ref) and inject it through local and global pathways: the local pathway retains time-resolved event cues, while an Audio Q-Former provides a clip-level acoustic-context condition. Third, jointly conditioning on multiple references can cause acoustic-attribute leakage across events. Localized reference attention and the TACO-Ref Router (TRR) explicitly constrain event-to-reference correspondence to reduce such interference. Experiments on VGGSound-Ref and VividBench demonstrate stronger reference controllability than existing V2A and exemplar-based methods while maintaining competitive Foley generation quality.
item.dc:creator: You Li, Dewei Zhou, Fan Ma, Dongliang He, Yi Yang

item.title: Lossless Re-Encoding of Vorbis and Opus Audio Files
item.description: arXiv:2611.32641v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We present Balrogg, a lossless recompressor that replaces the entropy coding of Ogg Vorbis and Ogg Opus files with adaptive context mixing models. For Vorbis, we write each represent each codebook entry as a tuple of small signed integers (digits), binarized in five stages, and mixed with a direct context model, a bit-history model, and a match model, with weights selected by the neighboring digits and the previous residue pass. For Opus, each symbol is coded by an adaptive context model initialized with the codec's probability tables as priors, and the pyramid vector quantizer (PVQ) indices of the CELT layer are split recursively into pulse counts. At the default level, Balrogg reduces Vorbis music by 16.2\%, Vorbis speech by 10.6%, and Opus speech by 5.4%; xz, zstd, ZPAQ, and bzip3 save at most 4.1% on the same files. Over 48 encoder configurations, files shrink to 66.5--96.1% of their size. Encoding and decoding are symmetric, run at 1.8--3.2~MB/s per core, and use less than 12~MiB of memory.
item.dc:creator: Kamila Szewczyk

item.title: Cif-query bridging for audio-native asr transfer to visual speech recognition
item.description: arXiv:2611.32697v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Audio-native automatic speech recognition (ASR) models provide strong speech-language priors, but their compact acoustic interfaces are mismatched with long, frame-level visual features. We propose CIF-Query Bridge, a lightweight connection from a Paraformer visual speech recognition (VSR) encoder to Qwen3-ASR. The existing visual continuous integrate-and-fire (CIF) predictor produces an input-dependent number of token-rate queries; a two-layer cross-attention bridge refines them against the complete frame sequence, and a linear adapter feeds the pretrained ASR projector and decoder. This design preserves access to uncompressed visual context while avoiding direct autoregressive processing of hundreds of video frames. On CMLR, the complete visual-only transfer system achieves 7.97% character error rate, compared with 11.78% for native Paraformer under the same test split and scoring protocol---a 3.81-point absolute and 32.3% relative reduction. Controlled ablations characterize bridge depth, projector initialization, adapter capacity, and CTC supervision. The results show that CIF-derived adaptive queries provide a compact interface for transferring audio-native ASR capability to VSR.
item.dc:creator: Chang Sun, Dongliang Xie, Wanpeng Xie, Bo Qin, Hong Yang

item.title: ToneMamaba: Learning Contextualized Tonal Contours with Boundary-Reset State Space Models
item.description: arXiv:2611.31267v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Mandarin tone recognition in connected speech is challenging because contextual and durational variation reshapes F0 contours. We propose ToneMamba, a boundary-aware state space model that replaces static boundary embeddings with bidirectional state resets at syllable, word, and IPU levels. Fixed weights fuse multi-level representations, while shared-weight bidirectional scans use channel-wise directional fusion to reduce parameters. Dynamic syllable pooling forms tonal contours, and rhythm-conditioned gating incorporates durational information. ToneMamba achieves 97.9% and 74.8% accuracy on FCU-VOICE-360 read and MCDC-8 conversational speech, outperforming the baseline (ToneNet) by 0.9 and 15.9 percentage points, respectively. Ablations show that word-level resets are particularly effective, while rhythm conditioning provides greater gains in conversational speech, underscoring the role of durational variation in spontaneous speech.
item.dc:creator: Po-Yu Chiu, Yi-Fen Liu

item.title: Lexical Tone and Word Order Matter in Translation: Prosodic Correspondence Across Languages
item.description: arXiv:2611.31276v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Prosody conveys emphasis, emotion, and intent, yet its correspondence across translation remains underexplored, especially when languages differ in lexical tone and word order. To our knowledge, we present the first systematic word-level analysis of prosodic correspondence in translated speech spanning tonal and non-tonal Asian languages, with comparisons to European-language findings and explicit analyses of lexical tone and word reordering. Building on prior evidence of fine-grained prosody correspondence in European-language pairs, we investigate how these linguistic factors relate to word-level pitch and energy correspondence between English and five languages: Mandarin Chinese, Thai, and Vietnamese, which have lexical tone, and Japanese and Korean as additional comparisons. Correspondence is generally lower than previously reported European-language estimates. Adjusting for lexical tone increases pitch correspondence for English-Mandarin Chinese, English-Thai, and English-Vietnamese. However, English-Japanese and English-Korean also exhibit lower correspondence than the European-language estimates, indicating that tonal status alone does not explain the observed pattern. Greater word reordering is associated with weaker local correspondence even under semantic alignment, suggesting that semantic alignment does not fully account for differences in prosodic organization. These findings characterize the limits of fine-grained acoustic correspondence across translation and motivate prosody modeling that accounts for lexical pitch constraints and the structural context of translated content.
item.dc:creator: Haopeng Xie, Ismail Rasim Ulgen, Shengying Zhao, Berrak Sisman, Philipp Koehn

item.title: MOZAIC: An Audio-Video Deepfake Benchmark for Telling What Is Fake
item.description: arXiv:2611.31301v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Audio-video (AV) deepfakes can fake the face, the voice, or both. Most benchmarks only ask whether a clip is real or fake, so they cannot show whether a detector relies on the picture, the voice, or encoding traces. We present MOZAIC, a paired benchmark with a 4-way label in which every source clip is released in all four combinations of real or fake video and real or fake audio so each modality contribution can be measured directly. Fakes cover inner-face swapping, whole-frame video diffusion and voice conversion. MOZAIC has 137,745 clips from 15,014 source pairs and four tasks: T1 AV authenticity, T2 manipulation type, T3 identity verification and T4 explanation. We evaluate 12 AV multimodal LLMs (MLLMs), train four detectors and fine-tune MLLMs with LoRA. Overall, the best MLLM reaches only 35.6% on the four-way T1 and catches far more video-only fakes than voice-only fakes (43.6% vs 7.5%). Trained detectors reach 98.4% on T1, and LoRA fine-tuning raises explanation scores (OmniVinci 4.17 to 7.40, Qwen2.5-Omni 4.42 to 6.98), but the best T1 detector falls to 78.3% when the face-swap generator is held out of training, so generalization and explanation remain open. We release the dataset, the compact MOZAIC-SMALL split, the code and the prompts. https://vectorinstitute.github.io/mozaic/
item.dc:creator: Shaina Raza, Mohamed Hafez, Ahmed Y. Radwan, Khalid Elgazzar, Kathryn Hume

item.title: BEARING: Who Is Talking to Whom? Grounding Acoustic Direction in Vision for Online Multi-Party Conversation
item.description: arXiv:2611.31735v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Understanding a group conversation means deciding, from video and audio, who is speaking and to whom. Leading systems treat these tasks offline on single-channel clips and align models with a self-evaluation reward. We propose BEARING, a geometry-first alternative built on one measured signal: the direction from which a microphone array beside the camera hears a sound. A label-free calibration learned from the stream registers this direction into the camera image, and an online registry of faces, voices and directions needs no enrollment. The registered direction serves as (i) a visual prompt for a vision-language model, a marker on the speaker or an arrow toward an off-screen source; (ii) one input of a reliability-weighted fusion with visual active-speaker detection, for speakers in the same direction from the array; and (iii) a verifiable reward for alignment: the named speaker must sit where the sound comes from, the confidence must match that check, and always answering "group" earns nothing. Every decision is online, with the lookahead as an explicit parameter. On 9,498 addressee-labelled utterances from three AMI sites and egocentric EasyCom, the direction prompt raises speaker accuracy from 54% to 74%; addressee accuracy moves by about two points, because telling one addressee from the group depends on the words more than on where people are. For co-located speakers on AVDIAR, visual active-speaker detection holds 95% where direction alone falls to 59%. The verifiable reward beats self-evaluation under GRPO, reward-ranked fine-tuning and DPO; shrinking the lookahead from 5 s to 0.5 s costs 4.5 DER points on AMI, and learning the registration online costs a dip in the first two minutes before the system overtakes vision alone. Code and evaluation protocols will be released.
item.dc:creator: Nader Lobandi, Lombe Chileshe, Mohammad Mehdi Hosseini, Mohammad H. Mahoor

item.title: SynAVID: A Synthetic Audio-Visual Immersive Dataset of Dynamic Scenes
item.description: arXiv:2611.32311v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Immersive scene modeling requires synchronized visual and auditory observations under changing viewpoints and scene conditions. Obtaining such observations and references for controlled scene changes remains challenging. We introduce SynAVID, a synthetic audio-visual immersive dataset comprising eight indoor and outdoor scenes. Each minute-scale episode combines fixed camera arrays and moving trajectories with synchronized, viewpoint-dependent binaural audio. Shared scene dynamics, sound-source events, and observer poses drive visual rendering and geometry-aware acoustic synthesis. We evaluate existing methods for visual reconstruction, binaural audio reconstruction, and audiovisual editing. Mixed-observation configurations generally improve visual reconstruction on fixed and moving test views, while transiently occupied and sparsely observed regions remain challenging. Methods rank differently on spectral, interaural, and perceptual audio metrics. Geometric and instance annotations expose uneven observation support and local Gaussian representations beyond aggregate scores. Paired references assess target edits and surrounding content, while controlled geometry changes produce listener-dependent acoustic responses. The project page is available at https://avery-xu.github.io/synavid-project/.
item.dc:creator: Jun Xu, Sujing Li, Chunhao Bi, Zhengxue Cheng, Ronghua Wu, Qunshan Gu, Li Song

item.title: Phoneme-identity depth profiles do not reliably predict LoRA placement for dysarthric ASR
item.description: arXiv:2611.32455v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Parameter-efficient adaptation of a speech foundation model to dysarthric speech requires a rarely justified choice: which encoder layers to adapt. A recently proposed strategy is to probe the encoder, find where phonetic information becomes most decodable, and put the adapters there. We test that inference across two ASR models (Qwen3-ASR, Whisper-small) and two dysarthric corpora (Mandarin CDSD, English UASpeech), holding recipe and seed discipline constant. The inference fails. Measured under one pipeline rather than inherited from published figures, all four phoneme-error curves minimise between 83% and 92% of relative depth, each model's minimising layer moving no further between corpora than between probe seeds. The best adaptation band is not similarly constant: none of three natural mappings from the curve to a band -- steepest improvement, lowest band-mean error, or knee location -- recovers the best tested configuration. We do not claim no statistic of the curve could work, only that these three do not. Placement still matters, but is model- and corpus-specific. On CDSD the models disagree -- Qwen3-ASR prefers its upper third (29.88% CER, three-seed mean), Whisper-small all-block LoRA (53.56%) -- while on UASpeech neither favours the upper band. At three seeds, upper-versus-all is resolved (-1.31 pp, CI [-2.16, -0.25]) but upper-versus-middle is not (-0.83 pp, CI [-2.06, +1.86]). The two models' preferences differ as a directly tested interaction (-4.71 pp, CI [-6.17, -2.89]); we designate this the primary claim, and record that the designation was made post hoc. On Qwen3-ASR x UASpeech, adapting near the input is reliably worse than not adapting at all (+9.90 pp CER). We recommend choosing the band by a short adaptation sweep on the model and corpus in hand, not by reading it off a probe.
item.dc:creator: Bernard Muller, LaVonne Roberts

item.title: ClusterVAD: Threshold-Free Unsupervised Voice Activity Detection with Pre-Trained Neural Representations
item.description: arXiv:2611.33059v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Voice activity detection (VAD) is one of the first steps in speech processing pipelines, from transcription and diarization to speech language models. Supervised detectors need labelled data and inherit the domain and annotation conventions of their training corpora. Existing unsupervised detectors rely on hand-crafted acoustic features which cannot benefit from data and degrade in far-field, noisy or atypical speech. We propose ClusterVAD, an unsupervised VAD built on frozen speech foundation model representations. Fitted once on a small set of untranscribed speech, it clusters the representations and labels each cluster as speech or non-speech with sonority, an acoustic measure. At inference, a frame-level speech probability is computed from the cluster assignments, and a two-state hidden Markov model fitted to each recording enables threshold-free detection. Across benchmarks covering meetings, far-field and noisy recordings, Mandarin and dysarthric speech, ClusterVAD obtains the lowest detection error on pause-level references and is competitive on speaker turn-level references. These results indicate that speech foundation models inherently capture the distinction between speech and non-speech, which can be leveraged without training a detector.
item.dc:creator: Karl El Hajal, Mathew Magimai. -Doss

item.title: DiaCap: Jointly Learning Who Speaks When for Audiovisual Dialogue Captioning
item.description: arXiv:2611.33153v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: We present DiaCap, an audiovisual LLM for comprehensive dialogue captioning, which produces the transcript, timestamps, and a visual description of the speaker for every utterance in a video. Considering that utterance timing and audiovisual diarization are tightly coupled, DiaCap unifies the tasks in a single model, trained in two complementary stages. First, we train DiaCap on 225K curated clips, using synthetic captions that densely label every utterance in detail. Second, we further refine the model via reinforcement learning on 2.9K human-corrected clips, using fine-grained feedback that directly evaluates utterance timing, speaker grouping, and speaker binding. On DiaDemBench, which we extend with utterance-level timestamps and subtitle redaction, both DiaCap with off-the-shelf transcripts and its end-to-end variant DiaCap-E2E achieve strong results. Specifically, DiaCap performs on par with Gemini 4 Argon in audiovisual diarization while clearly outperforming it in timestamp accuracy (76.59 vs. 42.76 TIME). It also maintains strong diarization on multilingual and minute-long videos, and transfers to audiovisual question answering.
item.dc:creator: Binfei Ji, Zhiwen Cao, Anqi Yang, Prem Seetharaman, Shuo Yang, Ratheesh Kalarot, Yingyan Celine Lin, Mingze Xu

item.title: S3-S2ST: Semantically Supervised Streaming Speech-to-Speech Translation
item.description: arXiv:2610.36777v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Streaming speech-to-speech translation requires timely decisions about when partial input is sufficient for accurate translation. We present S3-S2ST, a model that learns to translate and speak from semantically aligned streaming supervision. By converting utterance-level speech pairs into incremental training examples, we teach a learned policy when to commit translations. Its adjustable threshold controls the quality--latency tradeoff on a fixed 640\,ms input grid. S3-S2ST delivers competitive English--Chinese translation on FLEURS and leads the evaluated streaming systems in translation quality on the internal 9-pair test set. On RealSI, adapting the threshold to buffered speech further improves quality over a low fixed threshold with little change in first-audio latency. We have released the training and inference code and 4B model weights at https://github.com/QwenAudio/S3-S2ST
item.dc:creator: Yuxiang Zhao, Zhiyun Fan, Yu Pu, Yanjie An, Yushen Chen, Wenrui Liang, Baiji Liu, Yunchong Xiao, Zhaoci Liu, Keqi Deng, Kai Yu, Zhifu Gao, Xiangang Li, Xie Chen

item.title: PairAlign: A Framework for Autoregressive Tokenization via Self-Alignment with Applications to Audio Tokenization
item.description: arXiv:2605.06582v5 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Modern learning systems represent perceptual signals with continuous vectors, but comparison, retrieval, memory, alignment, and reasoning are often symbolic. In language, tokens provide this interface; for speech and audio, it must be learned. Existing audio tokenizers rely on local quantization, clustering, or reconstruction, leaving sequence consistency, compactness, length, termination, and edit geometry only indirectly controlled. We introduce PairAlign, a framework for compact audio tokenization through autoregressive self-alignment. An encoder maps speech to a continuous condition, and an autoregressive decoder emits tokens from BOS to EOS. Given two content-preserving views, PairAlign derives a canonical anchor target and trains both views to predict it, with unrelated in-batch targets as competing sequences. It first learns an autoregressive bridge from VQ targets and then transitions to EMA-teacher self-alignment with grounding and anti-collapse controls. On 3 s speech, PairAlign produces shorter, non-degenerate sequences while retaining ordered paired-view consistency. On the TIMIT retrieval archive, it operates at 8.28 tokens/s, reducing archive token count by 70.65% and the edit-distance work proxy by 91.87% relative to Stage I. Positive-negative probes show strong separation across phone-disjoint, trigram-disjoint, and temporally rearranged negatives, while rate-controlled post-hoc BPE does not recover the same compactness-consistency operating point. These results expose a rate-granularity trade-off: PairAlign does not uniformly outperform denser tokenizers on every local metric, but provides a lower-rate symbolic interface preserving ordered and relational structure. Conceptually, PairAlign follows JEPA-style predictive learning by predicting an abstract target rather than reconstructing the input; here, the target is a learned variable-length symbolic sequence.
item.dc:creator: Adhiraj Banerjee, Vipul Arora
